facts.claim: ADA Practical Guide thresholds for adult outpatient dental care: under 160/100: no modification for elective or emergency care. Over 160/100: repeat the reading; if it comes down, or is within a physician's written guidance, proceed; if confirmed, no elective care and refer to the physician. Emergency care at a confirmed 160-180 systolic and/or 100-109 diastolic when pain is driving the BP: treat, check BP every 10-15 minutes, use anxiety reduction. Confirmed >180 systolic and/or >109 diastolic: consult the physician before proceeding. Systolic >180 and/or diastolic >100: refer as soon as possible, or urgent medical evaluation if symptomatic.
facts.conditions: The ADA table itself is inconsistent: its body uses >109 diastolic for "consult before proceeding", its footnote >100 for "refer as soon as possible". Key items on the body thresholds (160/100 and 180/109) and avoid diastolic values of 101-109 where the two disagree.

facts.claim: Staging, unchanged from 2014: At risk: no apparent necrotic bone, asymptomatic, treated with IV or oral antiresorptives. Stage 0 (nonexposed variant): no clinical necrotic bone, but nonspecific symptoms or clinical/radiographic findings: unexplained odontalgia, dull jaw ache that may radiate to the TMJ, sinus pain, altered sensation; tooth loosening not explained by periodontitis, intraoral or extraoral swelling; alveolar bone loss not explained by periodontitis, sclerotic trabecular pattern, no new bone in extraction sockets, osteosclerosis, thickened lamina dura and narrowed PDL space. Up to 50% progress to stage 1. Stage 1: exposed necrotic bone or a fistula probing to bone, asymptomatic, no infection. Stage 2: the same with infection/inflammation, symptomatic. Stage 3: stage 2 plus one or more of: necrosis beyond the alveolar bone (inferior border or ramus of the mandible; maxillary sinus or zygoma), pathologic fracture, extraoral fistula, oral-antral or oral-nasal communication, osteolysis to the inferior border of the mandible or the sinus floor.

facts.claim: Risk by indication: much higher in cancer (<5%) than in osteoporosis (<0.05%). Cancer: zoledronate risk is 2-10 times placebo; ranges about 1.6-4% after 2 years and 3.8-18% beyond 2 years of treatment (Ng et al. review); denosumab 0-6.9% (most studies <5%), 1.9% under 24 months and 6.9% over 24 months of exposure, comparable to zoledronate. Osteoporosis: IV zoledronate <=0.02% (<=2 per 10,000); oral bisphosphonates <=0.05% (<=5 per 10,000); denosumab 0.3% after 10 years (almost an order of magnitude higher than bisphosphonates); romosozumab 0.03-0.05%. Placebo groups in osteoporosis trials: 0-0.02%.

facts.claim: Drug holidays: still controversial; the 2022 working group could not reach consensus (split evenly between case-by-case holidays using prior recommendations and never offering them). Denosumab in osteoporosis: stopping risks rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures; if held, do the surgery 3-4 months after the last dose and restart 6-8 weeks after surgery. facts.claim: Oxygen in COPD is given with caution, not withheld: in COPD the respiratory center becomes tolerant to high carbon dioxide and breathing is driven by low oxygen tension (hypoxemic drive), so too much oxygen can remove the stimulus to breathe and cause apnea, especially in a patient who is asleep or unconscious. CNS depressants are used cautiously in COPD; Becker singles out opioids (which depress the central carbon dioxide drive) and inhalation anesthetics (which have a profound effect on the peripheral hypoxemic drive). facts.claim: Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness caused by transient global cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, short duration and spontaneous, complete recovery. Vasovagal syncope (the "common faint") is a reflex syncope set off by emotion or orthostatic stress; in the dental office pain, fear and anxiety trigger a reflex bradycardia and hypotension that reduce cerebral blood flow. It is usually preceded by prodromal symptoms of autonomic activation (sweating, pallor, nausea).

facts.claim: Vasovagal syncope is the most common medical emergency in dental practice. Young adult men (about 16-35 years) are at higher risk; other contributors include prolonged sitting or standing, hypoglycemia, fatigue and humid, overcrowded rooms.

facts.claim: Recognizing vasovagal syncope: the presyncope phase brings warmth in the face or neck, pallor, cold sweat, dilated pupils, hyperpnea (increased breathing), cold extremities and tachycardia; then bradycardia and hypotension, with dizziness and visual disturbance, develop just before consciousness is lost. While unconscious the patient may breathe irregularly (or stop breathing) and show convulsive twitching from cerebral hypoperfusion. After waking the patient may be briefly confused, and pallor, nausea, weakness and sweating can last for hours.
facts.conditions: Narrative review (citing Malamed). Brief jerking during a faint does not by itself mean a seizure; prolonged unconsciousness does call for other diagnoses (SYN-6).

cites.quote: Patients may initially experience warmth in the face or neck, pallor, and cold sweats. Other signs include pupillary dilation, hyperpnea, cold extremities, and tachycardia
Bradycardia and hypotension may develop immediately before syncope, accompanied by dizziness and visual disturbances.
During the loss of consciousness, breathing may become irregular or apneic.
Cerebral hypoperfusion can cause convulsive movements or muscular twitching
Patients may experience transient confusion or disorientation after regaining consciousness.
Postsyncopal symptoms, such as pallor, nausea, weakness, diaphoresis, and abnormal vital signs, may persist for several hours

facts.claim: Managing vasovagal syncope (P-C-A-B-D): at the first sign, place the patient supine with the legs level with or slightly above the head (a full Trendelenburg tilt of 15-30 degrees is controversial); the main danger while unconscious is airway obstruction from muscle relaxation, so check the carotid pulse, open the airway with a head-tilt, chin-lift and confirm breathing. Supine positioning with the legs raised usually brings recovery.
facts.conditions: Dental narrative review (Li and Ouanounou 2026, citing ADA/Malamed) and a CE review (Becker 2014). The general P-C-A-B-D frame: EM-4.

cites.quote: The standard management approach for vasovagal syncope in dental settings follows the P–CAB–D protocol
support placing the patient in a supine position with the legs level with or slightly elevated above the head at the earliest sign of syncope to improve venous return
The Trendelenburg position, in which the feet are elevated 15–30° above the head, remains controversial
The greatest concern in syncope is airway obstruction caused by generalized muscular relaxation
A patent airway should be established using the head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
Circulation is assessed by palpating the carotid pulse
breathing should be confirmed by observing chest rise, listening for breath sounds, and feeling airflow
Primary assessment and reclining the patient with legs elevated generally results in recovery.

facts.claim: If a fainted patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally, or has no palpable pulse, start basic life support (CPR, AED) and activate EMS. Otherwise give supportive care: oxygen, vital signs every 5 minutes compared with baseline, and loosen tight clothing (ties, belts). Drugs are not routinely needed, because most episodes resolve with positioning and supportive care.
facts.conditions: Narrative review. Oxygen flow rates (6-10 L/min conscious, 10-15 L/min by bag-valve mask unconscious) come from this one review: do not key them. CPR details: EM-5.

cites.quote: If the patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally, or has no palpable pulse, basic life support, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation and automated external defibrillator use, should be initiated promptly, and emergency medical services should be activated.
Oxygen is administered at 6–10 L/min for conscious patients or at 10–15 L/min via a bag-valve mask for unconscious patients
Vital signs should be monitored every 5 min and compared with baseline values to assess recovery.
Loosening tight clothing, including ties and belts, can improve venous return and cerebral perfusion during recovery.
Adjunct pharmacological therapy is not routinely indicated because most syncopal episodes resolve with appropriate positioning and supportive care.

facts.claim: Delayed recovery from an apparent faint (more than about 2 minutes to regain consciousness, or more than 15-20 minutes to recover fully) points to another cause: hyperventilation, hypoglycemia, anemia or seizure. Check blood glucose promptly in a patient with diabetes. Warning features that call for medical evaluation include fainting during exertion or while lying down, no obvious trigger, a family history of sudden cardiac death, slow recovery, and unexplained syncope without a prodrome in patients under 10 or over 40.
facts.conditions: Time cutoffs come from a narrative review (Li and Ouanounou 2026, citing Runser 2017 and Malamed). The same review says post-syncope symptoms can last hours (SYN-3), so key the 2-minute delay to regain consciousness, not the 15-20 minute full-recovery figure, as the warning sign. The alarming-symptom list is from the ESC 2009 guideline, since replaced by the 2018 ESC guideline (not openly fetchable). Hypoglycemia management: DM-3 to DM-5.

cites.quote: If recovery is delayed (> 2 min to regain consciousness or > 15–20 min for complete recovery), potential differential diagnoses include hyperventilation, hypoglycemia, anemia, or seizure activity
Blood glucose levels should be promptly assessed in patients with diabetes and managed accordingly.

cites.loc: Part 5.1: Management of syncope in general practice
cites.quote: Alarming symptoms are: syncope during exertion, syncope in the lying position, absence of external factors, family history of SCD, or slow recovery from syncope
Patients aged < 10 years or > 40 years with unexplained syncope without prodromal symptoms require urgent cardiovascular and neurological evaluation.

facts.claim: After a vasovagal episode, remove the trigger (needles, bloody instruments) and do not continue dental treatment at the same visit, because recurrence is more likely in the post-syncope phase. Low-risk patients may go home with a responsible escort; high-risk patients (see SYN-6) are referred for hospital evaluation.
facts.conditions: Narrative review; "generally discouraged", not an absolute rule.

cites.quote: Triggers, such as needles or blood-contaminated instruments, should be removed to prevent recurrence.
Because the postsyncopal phase carries an increased risk of recurrence, continuation of dental treatment during the same visit is generally discouraged
Low-risk patients may be discharged with a responsible escort, whereas high-risk patients should be referred to a hospital for further evaluation.

facts.claim: Preventing vasovagal syncope: screen new patients for dental anxiety (e.g., Corah Dental Anxiety Scale); give local anesthetic with the patient supine, with topical anesthetic, a buffered/warmed solution and a slow injection (about 1 cartridge per minute); consider nitrous oxide or oral diazepam for a moderately anxious patient or one with a history of fainting; teach patients to recognize prodromal symptoms and abort an episode by lying down or with physical counterpressure maneuvers (leg crossing, leg raising).
facts.conditions: Dental specifics are from a narrative review; the counterpressure evidence cited there for dentistry is a small pilot study (7 of 8 patients). ESC 2009 makes education, reassurance and PCMs the cornerstone of reflex syncope therapy.

cites.quote: New patients should be screened for dental anxiety using validated instruments, such as the Corah Dental Anxiety Scale
Best practices to minimize discomfort include supine positioning; buffering and warming the anesthetic solution; topical anesthesia; slow injection rates (approximately 1 cartridge/min)
Conscious sedation with nitrous oxide or oral diazepam is effective in patients with moderate anxiety or a history of syncope
Physical counterpressure maneuvers, including leg raising and leg crossing, improve hemodynamic stability
early recognition of prodromal symptoms, and performing manoeuvres to abort the episode [e.g. supine posture, physical counterpressure manoeuvres (PCMs)]

facts.claim: Persistent vasovagal bradycardia with hypotension (rare): atropine 0.5 mg counters the vagal slowing and can be repeated up to 3 mg total (Becker, dental emergency kit: sublingual or IM every 5 minutes; Li and Ouanounou, citing the European Resuscitation Council: IV every 3-5 minutes). Doses below 0.5 mg can paradoxically slow the heart further. If the patient is hypotensive with a normal heart rate, atropine is ineffective and a vasopressor such as ephedrine is used instead.
facts.conditions: Dental CE review (Becker 2014) and narrative review (Li and Ouanounou 2026, citing ERC IV dosing). The AHA 2020 adult bradycardia algorithm uses 1 mg IV (not quoted here): do not key 0.5 mg as wrong or right against 1 mg, and name the source in any stem that keys a dose, route or interval. Ephedrine doses differ (Becker 25 mg IM/sublingual; Li and Ouanounou 5 mg IV up to 50 mg): do not key an ephedrine dose. These drugs are rarely needed (SYN-5).

cites.quote: However, in rare cases the episode persists, and drugs may be indicated to counter the event.
When bradycardia is present atropine should be administered.
atropine 0.5 mg IV every 3–5 min, up to a maximum dose of 3 mg, for adults with symptomatic bradycardia
Doses lower than 0.5 mg may be associated with paradoxical vagotonic effects that result in further slowing of heart rate.
If hypotension is accompanied by a normal heart rate, any further increase in rate is unlikely to improve blood pressure, so atropine is ineffective. In this case ephedrine is ideal.
Atropine can be injected sublingually or IM in doses of 0.5 mg (0.5 mL)
The dose can be repeated every 5 minutes up to 3 mg total based on heart rate and blood pressure readings.

facts.claim: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension: blood pressure drops when the patient stands up, for example after a long dental procedure; it affects about 20% of adults over 60, with autonomic dysregulation, low blood volume and medication side effects contributing. Confirm stable vital signs and bring the patient upright gradually. If the patient faints, manage it like vasovagal syncope: check consciousness, place supine, then C-A-B.
facts.conditions: Narrative review. Medication causes are listed in its Table 1 (diuretics; vasodilators such as calcium channel blockers, nitrates and alpha blockers; antidepressants): not quoted, since the table text is split across lines. Risk groups for orthostatic hypotension: BP-5.

cites.quote: Orthostatic hypotension occurs when blood pressure drops upon standing, such as after a long dental procedure.
This condition affects approximately 20% of adults aged > 60 years, with contributing factors including autonomic dysregulation, hypovolemia, and medication side effects
Stable postoperative vital signs should be confirmed before the patient is gradually returned to an upright position.
Orthostatic hypotension is managed using a protocol similar to that for vasovagal syncope.
Patients are assessed for consciousness, positioned supine, and managed according to the CAB protocol.

facts.claim: Hyperventilation syndrome, often driven by anxiety or panic: rapid, uncontrolled breathing with hypocapnia, dizziness and weakness; respiratory alkalosis can add tingling, numbness and tetany. Organic illness must be ruled out before calling it hyperventilation.
facts.conditions: Not quoted, do not key alone: the usual teaching that the patient stays conscious (a contrast with syncope), and which organic illnesses to exclude (e.g., asthma attack, hypoglycemia, cardiac causes). Hyperventilation is also a differential for delayed recovery from an apparent faint (SYN-6).

cites.quote: Rapid and uncontrolled breathing, Hypocapnia, dizziness, weakness
associated symptoms may be attributable to hyperventilation (increased minute ventilation) and respiratory alkalosis ( e.g. tingling, tetany and numbness)
Organic illness must be excluded before making a diagnosis of hyperventilation.
Patients with pure hyperventilation due to anxiety or panic attacks are unlikely to require oxygen therapy.

facts.claim: Managing hyperventilation in the chair: sit the patient upright and coach slow breathing. Supplemental oxygen is not needed when the oxygen saturation is normal or high (a dental review calls it contraindicated), and rebreathing from a paper bag is no longer advised because it can cause hypoxemia.
facts.conditions: Older dental texts teach paper-bag or cupped-hand rebreathing; BTS 2017 advises against it, so do not key the paper bag as correct. The "through one nostril" detail and "contraindicated" wording are from one narrative review (Li and Ouanounou 2026). Reassurance and benzodiazepines for severe cases are not covered by these quotes.

cites.quote: Place patient upright
Encourage slow breathing through one nostril
Supplemental O 2 is contraindicated
Those with normal or high SpO 2 do not require oxygen therapy.
Re-breathing from a paper bag may cause hypoxaemia and is not recommended.

facts.claim: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is abnormal kidney structure or function present for at least 3 months, with implications for health. KDIGO grades GFR (mL/min per 1.73 m2) as G1 90 or more (normal or high), G2 60-89 (mildly decreased), G3a 45-59 (mildly to moderately decreased), G3b 30-44 (moderately to severely decreased), G4 15-29 (severely decreased) and G5 under 15 (kidney failure). Without evidence of kidney damage, G1 or G2 alone does not meet the criteria for CKD.
facts.conditions: KDIGO also classifies CKD by cause and albuminuria category (A1-A3); this record covers only the GFR categories. Many textbooks call these 'stages 1-5'; KDIGO's term is GFR categories.

cites.quote: abnormalities of kidney structure or function, present for a minimum of 3 months, with implications for health
G1 Normal or high ≥90 G2 Mildly decreased 60–89 G3a Mildly to moderately decreased 45–59
G3b Moderately to severely decreased 30–44 G4 Severely decreased 15–29 G5 Kidney failure <15
In the absence of evidence of kidney damage, neither G1 nor G2

facts.claim: Prescribing for a patient with CKD (KDIGO 2024 practice points): people with CKD may be more susceptible to the nephrotoxic effects of medications, so weigh benefits against potential harms; consider GFR when dosing drugs cleared by the kidneys; and review and limit over-the-counter medicines and dietary or herbal remedies that may be harmful in CKD. Because the kidneys filter less, drugs can build up (NIDDK), so a provider may give a smaller dose, give it less often, or stop or switch the drug.

cites.quote: People with CKD may be more susceptible to the nephrotoxic effects of medications. When prescribing such medications to people with CKD, always consider the benefits versus potential harms.
Consider GFR when dosing medications cleared by the kidneys.
Review and limit the use of over-the-counter medicines and dietary or herbal remedies that may be harmful for people with CKD.

facts.claim: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) are nephrotoxic: they lower GFR by reducing prostaglandin-dependent kidney blood flow and can cause allergic interstitial nephritis and nephrotic syndrome, and they can lead to acute kidney injury, especially in people with kidney disease, diabetes or high blood pressure. KDIGO lists acetaminophen as the potential non-nephrotoxic alternative analgesic, and chronic over-the-counter NSAID use should be discouraged. The ibuprofen label does not recommend it in advanced renal disease; if it must be used, monitor renal function closely.
facts.conditions: KDIGO adds that judicious NSAID use under careful supervision of a nephrologist may be preferred to opioids, so key 'avoid NSAIDs as the routine dental analgesic in CKD and prefer acetaminophen', not 'NSAIDs are absolutely contraindicated'. One dental narrative review (Albagieh 2024, sdj-2024-renal-dental) lists acetaminophen among nephrotoxic drugs to avoid while also calling paracetamol the drug of choice; follow KDIGO. General NSAID cautions are in RX-2 and RX-7.

cites.quote: NSAIDs: nephrotoxic effects include a decrease in GFR through a reduction in prostaglandin-dependent kidney blood
allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN), and nephrotic syndrome725 Acetaminophen
Indiscriminate chronic OTC NSAID use has been associated with a higher risks of kidney failure compared with nonuse and should be discouraged.

cites.loc: Be careful about the over-the-counter medicines you take
cites.quote: can damage your kidneys and lead to acute kidney injury

cites.loc: Be careful about the over-the-counter medicines you take
cites.quote: especially in those with kidney disease, diabetes, and high blood pressure. Ibuprofen and naproxen are NSAIDs.

treatment with ibuprofen tablets is not recommended in these patients with advanced renal disease. If ibuprofen tablet therapy must be initiated, close monitoring of the patients renal function is advisable.
judicious NSAID use, under careful supervision of a nephrologist, may be preferred to other pain medications such as opioids that have stronger associations with adverse events

facts.claim: Amoxicillin in renal impairment (FDA label; adults, and children 3 months or older weighing more than 40 kg): no dose reduction is generally needed unless impairment is severe. With GFR under 30 mL/min, do not use the 875 mg dose; GFR 10-30 mL/min: 500 or 250 mg every 12 hours; GFR under 10 mL/min: 500 or 250 mg every 24 hours; hemodialysis: 500 or 250 mg every 24 hours, plus an additional dose both during and at the end of dialysis (amoxicillin can be removed by hemodialysis). The choice of 250 or 500 mg depends on the severity of the infection.
facts.conditions: These are treatment doses for infection. The label says nothing about the single 2 g prophylaxis dose (IE-5) in renal impairment; don't key a renal adjustment for it. The label's Highlights contain a typo ('GFR greater than 30 mL/min'); sections 2.5 and 8.6 say less than 30 mL/min. The renal table applies to adults and to children 3 months or older weighing more than 40 kg; don't key it for smaller children.

hemodialysis.extra_dose: during and at end of dialysis

cites.quote: Patients with impaired renal function do not generally require a reduction in dose unless the impairment is severe.
Renal impairment patients with a glomerular filtration rate of less than 30 mL/min should NOT receive the 875 mg dose.
GFR 10 to 30 mL/min 500 mg or 250 mg every 12 hours, depending on the severity of the infection GFR less than 10 mL/min 500 mg or 250 mg every 24 hours
Hemodialysis 500 mg or 250 mg every 24 hours, depending on severity of the infection Administer an additional dose both during and at the end of dialysis
Amoxicillin may be removed from circulation by hemodialysis.

facts.claim: Valacyclovir is dose-reduced by creatinine clearance in adults (FDA label). For cold sores (normally two 2 g doses 12 hours apart, 1 day only): CrCl 30-49 mL/min, two 1 g doses 12 hours apart; CrCl 10-29 mL/min, two 500 mg doses 12 hours apart; CrCl under 10 mL/min, a single 500 mg dose. Patients on hemodialysis take the recommended dose after hemodialysis.
facts.conditions: Adults only; the label has no data for children with creatinine clearance under 50 mL/min/1.73 m2.

cites.quote: Normal Dosage Regimen (Creatinine Clearance ≥50 mL/min) Creatinine Clearance (mL/min) 30-49 10-29 <10
Do not exceed 1 day of treatment. Two 2-gram doses taken 12 hours apart Two 1-gram doses taken 12 hours apart Two 500-mg doses taken 12 hours apart 500-mg single dose
Patients requiring hemodialysis should receive the recommended dose of valacyclovir tablets after hemodialysis.
Valacyclovir Tablets Dosage Recommendations for Adults with Renal Impairment

facts.claim: Doxycycline and lidocaine are little affected by renal impairment (FDA labels): doxycycline's serum half-life is not significantly different in severe renal impairment and is not changed by hemodialysis, and the rise in BUN that tetracyclines can cause (antianabolic effect) has not been seen with doxycycline in renal impairment. Renal dysfunction does not affect lidocaine kinetics, although its metabolites may accumulate.
facts.conditions: Neither label states a renal dose adjustment, but neither says 'never adjust'; key only 'little affected by renal impairment'. Implied contrast only: other tetracyclines can raise BUN in renal impairment; the doxycycline label does not give a rule for them, so don't key 'tetracycline is contraindicated in CKD' from this record. Lidocaine in liver disease is LIV-6.

cites.quote: Studies have shown no significant difference in serum half-life of doxycycline (range 18–22 hours) in individuals with normal and severely impaired renal function. Hemodialysis does not alter serum half-life.
The antianabolic action of the tetracyclines may cause an increase in BUN. Studies to date indicate that this does not occur with the use of doxycycline in patients with impaired renal function.
Renal dysfunction does not affect lidocaine kinetics but may increase the accumulation of metabolites.

facts.claim: Patients on hemodialysis receive heparin during dialysis, so invasive dental procedures are commonly scheduled on non-dialysis days, preferably the day after dialysis, to avoid its residual anticoagulant effect; consult the nephrologist before procedures.
facts.conditions: Rests on two narrative reviews (J Clin Med 2026; Saudi Dent J 2024), not a guideline; the 2026 review says high-quality evidence for this timing is limited. Teaching sources often explain it by heparin's short half-life; no quote here gives a half-life or an hour count, so don't key one.

cites.quote: Invasive dental procedures are commonly scheduled on non-dialysis days because of concerns regarding residual anticoagulant effects and bleeding risk associated with heparin administration during hemodialysis, although high-quality evidence supporting this practice remains limited
Dental care should be avoided on the day of treatment (prefer the day after the hemodialysis).
hemodialysis patients should avoid any dental procedure on the first day, and the best way is to consult with the nephrologist before starting any procedure

facts.claim: The preferred long-term hemodialysis access is an arteriovenous (AV) fistula, a surgical connection of an artery to a vein, usually in the arm. Protect the access arm: do not put a blood pressure cuff on it, and do not draw blood or place an IV in it unless the dialysis team says it is okay.
facts.conditions: An AV graft (a tube connecting an artery and a vein, usually in the arm) may be used when a fistula is not possible; a catheter in a large vein, often in the neck or chest, is used when dialysis must start quickly or while a fistula or graft is healing (NKF). NKF's arm-protection advice applies to any access arm.

cites.quote: The best type of long-term access is an AV fistula.
usually in your arm, to create an AV fistula
Do not let anyone use a blood pressure cuff on your access arm. Do not let anyone draw blood or place an IV in your access arm unless your dialysis team says it is okay.
Blood pressure cuff and IV medications should be avoided in the arm with a shunt.
A graft may be used when a fistula is not possible.
It may be used when dialysis needs to start quickly or while a fistula or graft is healing.

facts.claim: Bleeding and infection in CKD: patients with CKD have platelet dysfunction that prolongs bleeding, and anemia is common, exceeding 50% in advanced stages. Hemodialysis and kidney transplant patients are highly susceptible to infection. Before surgery, screen bleeding risk (hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelet count, bleeding time) in consultation with the physician.
facts.conditions: Narrative reviews only (Saudi Dent J 2024; J Clin Med 2026). The 2024 review also says antimicrobial prophylaxis 'should be considered' for hemodialysis patients; AHA/ADA do not list dialysis or AV access as an indication (IE-1 to IE-3), so don't key prophylaxis from this record.

cites.quote: CKD patients have platelet dysfunction, increasing the tendency to prolong bleeding
Anemia is a frequent and clinically significant complication of CKD, with prevalence increasing as glomerular filtration rate declines and exceeding 50% in advanced stages.
The renal transplant or hemodialysis patient is highly susceptible to infection, particularly immediately after surgery
Physician consultation about physical status and control level.
Screening for the bleeding disorder before surgery, including hemoglobin, bleeding time, hematocrit, and platelet count.

facts.claim: Kidney transplant: before transplantation, a dental evaluation with radiographs and completion of needed treatment (active caries, periodontal disease, extraction of nonrestorable teeth) removes infection sources before immunosuppression begins. After transplant, elective dental treatment is generally safer once immunosuppression is stabilized, typically 3 to 6 months after the transplant, with timing set with the transplant team.
facts.conditions: Narrative review (J Clin Med 2026); it notes much of this rests on expert consensus. The same review reports that most US transplant centers recommend antibiotic prophylaxis before dental care, based on consensus and survey data, not trials; ADA has no general recommendation for solid organ transplants (PJ-4), so don't key prophylaxis. Cyclosporine-related gingival overgrowth is in GE-1.

cites.quote: Its main goal is to detect and address any potential sources of oral infection, which could pose serious systemic risks once immunosuppressive therapy begins.

Pre-transplant dental evaluation includes a detailed clinical examination, dental radiographs, and completion of all necessary treatments—such as managing active carious lesions, treating periodontal disease, and extracting teeth that cannot be restored

Elective dental treatment is generally considered safer after stabilization of immunosuppressive therapy, typically three to six months after transplantation, although the optimal timing should be individualized in consultation with the transplant team.

facts.claim: Liver disease can lower plasma coagulation factor levels, so coagulation and hemostasis tests can be informative before any invasive dental procedure. Consult the patient's physician on the degree of liver impairment and on drug choices, since liver disease can alter the metabolism of some drugs.
facts.conditions: ADA gives no INR or platelet cutoff; see LIV-2 (why the INR is a poor bleeding predictor in cirrhosis) and LIV-3 (platelets). Oral signs are in HEP-2.

cites.quote: The degree of a patient's liver functional impairment can be determined via consultation with the medical physician, since liver disease has important implications for dental treatment.

Patients with liver disease may have decreased plasma coagulation factor concentrations; before any invasive procedure is performed in these patients, coagulation and hemostasis tests can be informative.
Liver disease may also result in alterations in the metabolism of certain drugs.

facts.claim: In cirrhosis, both coagulation and primary hemostasis are rebalanced (for platelet function, mainly by high von Willebrand factor levels), but the balance is unstable and can tip toward bleeding or thrombosis. The PT/INR and aPTT do not accurately describe hemostasis in cirrhosis and should not be used to predict bleeding; international guidelines do not recommend routine lab testing and correction of hemostatic factors before invasive procedures, preferring case-by-case decisions. In a large prospective study of decompensated cirrhosis, neither platelet count nor PT predicted procedure-related bleeding.
facts.conditions: From a 2026 review that summarizes current guidance (the AASLD, AGA and EASL documents themselves are not openly readable here). Traditional dental teaching and ADA (LIV-1) still say to get coagulation tests and consult the physician before surgery; items may key that step, but must not key 'the INR predicts bleeding in cirrhosis' or an INR cutoff for extractions in liver disease. In the same prospective study the review gives its highest bleeding figure for dental extractions (36.3%, vs 1.7-5.7% for other procedure types), so local hemostatic measures still matter; don't key the 36.3% figure itself.

cites.quote: prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time do not accurately describe hemostasis in patients with cirrhosis and should not be used to predict bleeding
both coagulation and primary hemostasis are rebalanced, though unstable, and may paradoxically tip toward hemorrhage or thrombosis
is rebalanced in cirrhosis, mainly due to the increased levels of the adhesive protein von Willebrand factor

International guidelines do not recommend the routine use of laboratory monitoring and management of hemostatic factors before invasive procedures, but suggest to consider decisions on a case-by-case basis in special settings
Neither platelet count nor PT predicted adverse outcomes.
Bleedings occurred after dental extractions (36.3%), common bedside procedures (2.9%), vascular interventions (4.4%), endoscopic interventions (1.7%), and percutaneous interventions (5.7%).

facts.claim: Platelets and dental surgery: a platelet count of 50,000/uL or more has traditionally been recommended before procedures that may bleed, such as extractions, and in many countries lower counts are corrected by platelet transfusion before surgery. A 2026 systematic review found more postoperative bleeding below 50,000/uL (12.9% vs 4.9%; risk ratio 2.95), mostly after oral surgery, but no evidence that a count under 50,000/uL is itself a contraindication to dental treatment; assess patients individually. For cirrhosis, an expert consensus set the lowest acceptable platelet count at 30 x 10^9/L (30,000/uL) for low-risk and 50 x 10^9/L (50,000/uL) for high-risk procedures; the same experts could not agree whether dental extractions are low- or high-risk.
facts.conditions: The review pooled thrombocytopenia from any cause (liver, hematologic, cancer), not only liver disease. Its evidence is case reports, case series, cohort studies and one trial; the risk ratio pools the 10 studies that had both a below- and an above-50,000 group with at least one bleed. The NIDCR oncology guide uses 75,000 for invasive dental care during chemotherapy (CH-2, CH-3); state the threshold in the stem or key 50,000 only as the traditionally recommended level. Don't key a cirrhosis platelet threshold specifically for extractions.

cites.quote: it has been recommended that the platelet levels are ≥ 50,000/μL
Hence the current practice in many countries is to correct thrombocytopenia with platelet transfusions before surgery
Bleeding rates for cases with platelet levels < 50,000/μL were 12.9%, and 4.9% for ≥ 50,000/μL. Risk ratio was 2.95

There is no evidence that platelet counts < 50,000/μL is a contraindication for dental interventions, although findings suggest higher postoperative bleeding rates, particularly in oral surgery. Patients should be assessed individually
agreement was reached on the lowest acceptable platelet count (30 × 10 9 /L and 50 × 10 9 /L for low- and high-risk procedures, respectively)
Those without agreement included the placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt, esophagogastroduodenoscopy with band ligation, liver biopsy, and dental extractions.
Six case reports, four case series, nine cohort studies and one trial fulfilled the inclusion.
allowing for pooled risk ratio analysis and heterogeneity assessments

facts.claim: OTC acetaminophen label: severe liver damage may occur if a person takes more than 4,000 mg of acetaminophen in 24 hours, takes it with other drugs containing acetaminophen, or has 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using it. People with liver disease should ask a doctor before use.
facts.conditions: 4,000 mg in 24 hours is the label's liver-damage warning threshold. This product's directions limit adults to 6 caplets (3,000 mg) in 24 hours unless a doctor directs, so don't key 4,000 mg as this label's daily maximum; the ADA guideline maximum of 4,000 mg/day is in RX-4. Reduced doses in cirrhosis are in LIV-5.

facts.claim: In cirrhosis, acetaminophen is the preferred analgesic but at a reduced daily dose: reviews recommend 2 to 3 g/day for long-term use (2014 review) or up to 2 g/day (2026 review), below the 4 g label maximum. NSAIDs are best avoided in cirrhosis because of the risk of renal impairment, hepatorenal syndrome and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. NIDDK tells people with cirrhosis to talk with their doctor before taking OTC pain relievers, including NSAIDs and acetaminophen.
facts.conditions: Rests on two narrative reviews; no guideline quote. They differ on the ceiling (2-3 g/day vs up to 2 g/day): key only 'reduced, about 2 g/day or less' or 'lower than the usual 4 g maximum', never 3 g/day as safe. The 2014 review's 2-3 g/day is for patients not actively drinking alcohol; active drinking needs more caution (LIV-4).

cites.quote: Paracetamol is safe in patients with chronic liver disease but a reduced dose of 2-3 g/d is recommended for long-term use.
paracetamol is the preferred analgesic in patients with liver disease including cirrhosis
are best avoided because of risk of renal impairment, hepatorenal syndrome, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage

facts.claim: Amide local anesthetics are metabolized by the liver. Use lidocaine with caution in hepatic disease: patients with severe hepatic disease cannot metabolize local anesthetics normally and are at greater risk of toxic plasma concentrations, and lidocaine's half-life may be prolonged two-fold or more in liver dysfunction. The articaine (Septocaine) label likewise advises caution in severe liver disease.
facts.conditions: Neither label gives a reduced cartridge maximum for liver disease; don't key a number. Label maximums are in LA-1.

facts.claim: Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder (about 1 in 1000 people). VWF carries factor VIII and helps platelets bind to exposed collagen. Type 1 is a mild to moderate quantitative deficiency of VWF, type 3 a near-complete absence, and type 2 a qualitative defect (subtypes 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N). Main symptoms are mucocutaneous bleeding (nosebleeds, easy bruising, heavy menstrual bleeding) and surgical bleeding, particularly after dental extractions.

Orthograde root canal treatment has no contraindications and is sometimes done on an unrestorable tooth to avoid a high-risk extraction in the irradiated field. Extractions, implants or other bone surgery in an irradiated site carry ORN risk: when in doubt, refer to a hospital setting, where the radiation dose to the specific site can be checked. AAPD (pediatric) advises managing patients at risk of ORN with the oncology team in the hospital setting and avoiding elective invasive procedures. Refer suspected ORN to secondary care for diagnosis and management. Avoid surgery in general practice for patients who have had a free-flap reconstruction; surgery close to a flap belongs in a hospital setting.
facts.conditions: UK primary-care review plus AAPD (pediatric) best practices. Hyperbaric oxygen and pentoxifylline evidence is in ORN-3.

facts.claim: AAPD best practices (2022), absolute neutrophil count (ANC) before dental treatment in a patient on immunosuppressive cancer therapy: over 2,000/mm3, no antibiotic prophylaxis needed; 1,000 to 2,000/mm3, use clinical judgment based on health status and the planned procedure; under 1,000/mm3, defer elective dental care, and for an emergency discuss with the medical team a course of antibiotics versus a single prophylactic dose. Unless advised otherwise, the AHA endocarditis regimen is an acceptable prophylaxis option.
facts.conditions: AAPD writes for pediatric patients; adult sources differ: the archived NIDCR guide (CH-2) postpones invasive care below ANC 1,000/mm3 or considers antibiotics, and IDSA/ASCO (CH-4) reserve prophylaxis for expected ANC <500/uL for 7 days or more. Decide with the oncologist.

cites.quote: 2,000/mm3: no need for antibiotic prophylaxis
1,000/mm3 to 2,000/mm3: Use clinical judgment based on the patient’s health status and planned procedures.
< 1,000/mm3: defer elective dental care
In dental emergencies, discuss management with a course of antibiotic therapy versus a single dose of antibiotics
Unless advised otherwise, the American Heart Association’s standard regimen to prevent endocarditis is an acceptable option for the immunocompromised patient.

facts.claim: AAPD best practices (2022), platelets: under 60,000/mm3, defer elective treatment and avoid invasive procedures when possible. Medically necessary care is best given in a hospital, after discussing supportive measures (platelet transfusions before and after surgery, bleeding control, admission) with the physician. Local hemostatic measures (sutures, hemostatic agents, pressure packs, microfibrillar collagen, topical thrombin, gelatin foams) may be used; systemic aminocaproic acid or tranexamic acid may be recommended by the hematologist/oncologist. If platelets are transfused, ask the hematologist whether a post-transfusion count is needed before starting.
facts.conditions: AAPD best practices are written for pediatric patients. Platelet floors differ by source: AAPD 60,000/mm3; archived NIDCR guide 75,000/mm3 (CH-2); many teaching sources 50,000/mm3 (CH-3). Always name the source when keying a number.

cites.quote: < 60,000/mm3: Defer elective treatment and avoid invasive procedures when possible.
dental treatment is required, a hospital setting is most appropriate
Discuss supportive measures (eg, platelet transfusions pre- and postoperatively, bleeding control, hospital admission and care) with the patient’s physician before proceeding.
Localized hemostatic measures to manage prolonged bleeding may be utilized (eg, sutures, hemostatic agents, pressure packs, microfibrillar collagen, topical thrombin and/or gelatin foams).
Systemic measures (eg, aminocaproic acid, tranexamic acid) may be recommended by the hematologist/oncologist.
the dentist should consult with the hematologist regarding the need for a posttransfusion platelet count before the commencement of dental treatment

facts.claim: There is no single evidence-based blood-count threshold for invasive dental care during cancer therapy. ADA notes that published minimum platelet and neutrophil thresholds varied by source, and a 2026 review found few prospective studies of optimal ANC or platelet thresholds. Before invasive treatment, consult the oncology team about current hematologic status (red cell, white cell and platelet counts).
facts.conditions: This is why CH-2, CH-5 and CH-6 carry stem_names: a stem that keys a numeric cutoff must name its source (NIDCR, AAPD).

cites.loc: Dental Treatment Considerations During Active Therapy
cites.quote: In the past, recommended minimum thresholds for platelet count and neutrophil count (i.e., white count) for patients undergoing active cancer therapy to receive invasive dental procedures had been published; however, these varied based on the published source.

cites.loc: Dental Treatment Considerations During Active Therapy
cites.quote: Consulting with the patient's oncologist/oncology team can help to determine the patient's current health status and ability to undergo invasive dental treatment, especially hematologic (red cell, white cell, platelet counts) status.
few prospective investigations assessing optimal thresholds for ANC, platelet counts, or inflammatory markers

facts.claim: Timing before immunosuppressive cancer therapy: ideally all dental care is finished first. AAPD: extractions as atraumatic as possible (no sharp bony edges, wound closure), ideally 3 weeks (at least 10 to 14 days) before cancer therapy starts; symptomatic nonvital permanent teeth get root canal treatment in a single visit at least 1 week before therapy. A 2026 review: treat oral infections at least 14 days before immunosuppressive therapy; chronic, asymptomatic lesions can wait until immune recovery.
facts.conditions: AAPD best practices are written for pediatric patients. Intervals differ by source: archived NIDCR 7-10 days before myelosuppressive chemotherapy (CH-1); AAPD 3 weeks or at least 10-14 days; 2026 review at least 14 days. Name the source when keying a number.

cites.quote: Ideally, all dental care should be completed before immunosuppressive therapy is initiated.
Surgical procedures must be as atraumatic as possible, with no sharp bony edges remaining and satisfactory closure of the wounds.
These extractions ideally are performed 3 weeks (or at least 10 to 14 days) before cancer therapy is initiated to allow for adequate healing.
Symptomatic nonvital permanent teeth ideally should receive root canal treatment in a single visit at least 1 week before initiation of immunosuppressive therapy
oral infections should ideally be completed at least 14 days before initiating immunosuppressive therapy to allow for tissue healing and monitoring for postoperative complications
Interventions on chronic, asymptomatic lesions (e.g., chronic periodontitis without signs of exacerbation) can be postponed until after immune recovery

facts.claim: During chemotherapy cycles, blood counts typically start falling 5 to 7 days after a cycle begins and stay low for about 14 to 21 days before returning to normal. During immunosuppression, defer elective dental care; place temporary restorations and delay nonacute treatment until hematologic status is stable. For a dental emergency, plan treatment with the physician, who recommends supportive therapy (antibiotics, platelet transfusions, analgesia).
facts.conditions: AAPD (pediatric) best practices. Exact nadir timing varies by regimen; confirm counts with the oncology team (CH-7).

cites.quote: typically start falling 5 to 7 days after the beginning of treatment cycle and stay low for approximately 14 to 21 days before rising again to normal levels
temporary restorations may be placed and nonacute dental treatment may be delayed until the patient’s hematological status is stable
During immunosuppression, elective dental care should be deferred.

If a dental emergency arises, the treatment plan should be discussed with the patient’s physician who will make recommendations for supportive medical therapies (eg, antibiotics, platelet transfusions, analgesia).

facts.claim: Which teeth to treat or extract before chemotherapy or stem cell transplant. NCI PDQ describes three protocols: complete (all dental disease treated before therapy); partial, used when there is too little time (manage apical periodontitis only if symptomatic with a lesion of 5 mm or more; extract only teeth with probing depth of 8 mm or more and/or Miller class III mobility, teeth expected to exfoliate within weeks, or symptomatic partially erupted third molars with pus); and minimal (treat only symptomatic problems). AAPD uses a broader rule: extract teeth with a poor prognosis (nonrestorable, pockets over 5 mm, significant bone loss, furcation involvement, mobility, infection) that cannot be treated definitively.
facts.conditions: Cutoffs differ by source (NCI 8 mm; AAPD over 5 mm; a radiation-focused review over 6 mm, ORN-8). Name the source when keying a number. The AAPD guidance is written for pediatric patients.

cites.quote: Complete protocols: All dental pathologies are treated before antineoplastic chemotherapy and HSCT are initiated.
Partial protocols: Teeth with apical periodontitis are managed only if they are symptomatic and if size of the periapical lesion is 5 mm or more.

Teeth are extracted only if they have severe periodontitis (probing depth of ≥8 mm) and/or Miller's Class III mobility, they are expected to exfoliate within a few weeks, or if partially erupted third molars are symptomatic and with purulence.
Minimal protocols: Patients are treated only if they are symptomatic.
Partial dental evaluation/treatment protocols may be appropriate when there is insufficient time for complete dental evaluation/treatment protocols.

Extraction is the treatment of choice for teeth with a poor prognosis (eg, nonrestorable teeth, periodontal pockets greater than 5 mm, significant bone loss, furcation involvement, mobility, infection) that cannot be treated by definitive periodontal therapy.

facts.claim: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT): complete dental treatment before the transplant and postpone elective dentistry until immune recovery, at least 100 days after transplant (longer with chronic GVHD). Remove orthodontic appliances before conditioning, and minimize denture use for the first 3 weeks after transplant (wear only when eating). After discharge, a dental exam and prophylaxis about 6 months after HSCT and every 6 months thereafter.
facts.conditions: The 100-day rule and the advice to complete dental treatment before transplant come from AAPD best practices (pediatric); the orthodontic-appliance, denture and 6-month follow-up advice comes from NCI PDQ.

cites.quote: Elective dentistry will need to be postponed until immunological recovery has occurred, at least 100 days following HCT.
This may be longer if chronic GVHD or other complications (eg, persistent immunodeficiency) are present.
all dental treatment should be completed before the patient undergoes HCT
Remove orthodontic appliances (e.g., brackets, wires, retainers) before conditioning.
Minimize denture use during first 3 weeks posttransplant.
Wear dentures only when eating.
see a dentist for a routine follow-up examination and dental prophylaxis approximately 6 months after a HSCT and every 6 months thereafter

facts.claim: Analgesics during high-dose cancer therapy: NCI says systemic analgesics are given for oral pain when topical anesthetics are not enough, but NSAIDs, which affect platelet adhesion and damage the gastric mucosa, are contraindicated, especially when thrombocytopenia is present.
facts.conditions: NCI PDQ context: oral mucositis pain in patients receiving high-dose chemotherapy or HSCT.

cites.quote: Systemic analgesics are administered when topical anesthetic strategies are not sufficient for clinical relief.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that affect platelet adhesion and damage gastric mucosa are contraindicated, especially if thrombocytopenia is present.

facts.claim: Home oral care during cancer therapy: brush twice daily with a soft, nylon-bristled toothbrush and a mild-flavored fluoride toothpaste; foam swabs are not a routine substitute because they do not clean teeth. Thrombocytopenia alone does not decide whether a patient can brush, but avoid toothpicks and water irrigators when the patient is pancytopenic. Avoid alcohol-containing mouthrinses; hydrogen peroxide is not for daily rinsing; bland rinses (0.9% saline, sodium bicarbonate or both) every 2 to 4 hours as needed; fluoride gel (1.1% neutral sodium fluoride or 0.4% stannous fluoride) once daily for 2 to 3 minutes.
facts.conditions: Chlorhexidine is often prescribed during neutropenia (NCI) but is not recommended to prevent oral mucositis (CH-14); keep the two purposes apart.

cites.quote: use a soft, nylon-bristled toothbrush
a mild-flavored fluoride toothpaste twice daily
Foam-swab brushes do not effectively clean teeth and should not be considered a routine substitute for a soft, nylon-bristled toothbrush.
Thrombocytopenia is not the sole determinant of oral hygiene as patients are able to brush without bleeding at widely different levels of platelet counts.
Toothpicks and water irrigation devices should not be used when the patient is pancytopenic to avoid tissue trauma.
It is recommended that mouthrinses containing alcohol be avoided.
Hydrogen peroxide solutions are not recommended for daily rinsing.
Bland mouthrinses such as 0.9% saline, sodium bicarbonate solution, or a mixture of the two can be used every 2 to 4 hours or as needed to alleviate mouth discomfort.
Fluoride gel products (1.1% neutral sodium fluoride or 0.4% unflavored stannous fluoride) can be used once daily for 2 to 3 minutes.
Chlorhexidine rinses are often prescribed for the duration of neutropenia.

facts.claim: Oral mucositis (MASCC/ISOO guidance as summarized by AAPD 2022): prevention includes good oral hygiene, bland rinses (saline or sodium bicarbonate), benzydamine mouthrinse, oral cryotherapy (cooling with ice for bolus chemotherapy with short-half-life drugs), palifermin (FDA approved for mucositis prevention with high-dose chemotherapy and total body irradiation before HSCT) and photobiomodulation. Not recommended: sucralfate, antimicrobial lozenges, chlorhexidine, pentoxifylline and GM-CSF mouthwash. Mixed 'magic mouthwash' lacks evidence and many experts do not recommend it. Timing: AAPD says mucositis usually begins 7 to 10 days after HSCT conditioning starts; NCI describes first signs 3 to 4 days after infusion of cycled chemotherapy or conditioning, with ulcers forming in the second week and worst between days 7 and 14.
facts.conditions: Pediatric best-practice summary of the adult MASCC/ISOO guideline. Benzydamine's main indication in the guideline is head and neck radiation (not quoted here); don't key its indication. Onset timing differs between AAPD and NCI; key 'worst in the second week (days 7-14)', not a single onset day.

in patients undergoing conditioning with high-dose chemotherapy and total body irradiation followed by HCT
antimicrobial lozenges, chlorhexidine, pentoxifylline, and granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor mouthwash for OM are not recommended
No sucralfate mouthwash.
